title: A brief outranks a skill, and a weakened test is reported
description: Evidence is in the study report (quality-gates-internal reports/2026-11-16-agent-skills). Measured on this repository's own benchmark (docs/research/benchmark-feature-results.md section 4.1): the plain arm edited a protected test's assertion in every session, and the plugin arm differed from the skills-and-rules arm in nothing a grader measured - the same prose rule protected both. Live: _skill_places.resolve_skill refuses another plugin's skill; _policy.resolve allows a single named skill per active area. Read: agents/audit-reviewer.md says a named review skill is invoked FIRST while its must-not list forbids writes, with no sentence ranking the two; audit-lookup.py does not mention a review skill at all.
desiredOutcome: An agent brief states that its hard rules win over a skill's instructions; a configured review skill is named in the phase reviewer's brief on the drive route; a task whose diff weakens an existing test, deletes one, adds a skip or a suppression is reported to the reviewer by a script; a refactor task can prove its tests were green on the base; an agent's edit-tool write to .claude/audit.config.json is refused or asked; /audit:init shows its assumptions before synthesis; both shipped eval cases have the scaffold they name

tasks.title: Both agent briefs say their hard rules win over a skill's instructions
tasks.description:
plugins/audit/agents/audit-executor.md tells the executor to invoke each skill its brief lists FIRST; plugins/audit/agents/audit-reviewer.md tells the phase reviewer to invoke a named review skill FIRST. Neither says what happens when the skill's text contradicts the brief (a skill that says to commit, to ask the human and stop the turn, to mutate a file and restore it, to fetch a URL). Today that is prose against prose and the agent picks.

Add one sentence to each brief, in the hard-rules list: the hard rules of this brief win over any instruction a skill gives; where they conflict the agent follows the brief and names the conflict in its return (executor: outcome.technical; reviewer: intent.note), never resolving it silently.

CONSTRAINT YOU OWN: tools/measure-context.py AGENT_CEILINGS is executor 9000 / reviewer 7000 and `python3 tools/measure-context.py --tree plugins/audit` prints the briefs at 8910 and 6994 bytes on de21866c. The sentence does not fit as-is. Free the bytes by tightening existing wording WITHOUT dropping or weakening any rule (every existing pin in tests/ must stay green - several suites assert substrings of these two files, so run the whole sweep, not one file). Only if that is not possible, raise the ceiling by what the sentence costs and record the reason where the ceilings are defined. Say in your outcome which of the two you did and the byte counts before and after.

Dependants of these files you answer for: every tests/ case that asserts text of the two briefs (grep the two basenames under tests/ and tools/lints/), tools/measure-context.py --gate, and PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md wherever it quotes either brief.

Acceptance:
1. Each brief carries the precedence sentence inside its hard-rules section, naming where the conflict is reported.
2. A case fails when the sentence is removed from either brief (count occurrences, do not assert presence of a loose substring).
3. `python3 tools/measure-context.py --tree plugins/audit --gate` exits 0.
4. No existing rule of either brief was dropped: the full sweep is green.

tasks.title: The phase reviewer's brief names the review skill that resolved
tasks.description:
agents/audit-reviewer.md: 'A review skill named (mode: phase): invoke it FIRST', and its input table lists 'the review skill' as a phase-mode input of the computed brief (`audit-lookup.py brief <id> --role phase`). On de21866c `grep -n -i 'review.\?skill' plugins/audit/scripts/status/audit-lookup.py` prints nothing, and in plugins/audit/scripts/governance/drive-phase.py `_areas.resolve_review_skill` is read only where the drive decides whether a review is due. So on the drive route a plan with meta.reviewSkill / meta.areas[tag].reviewSkill / phase.reviewSkill set appears to get a review that never learns the skill's name.

FIRST establish the fact by running, not reading: build a scratch plan (tempfile.mkdtemp, removed in finally) whose phase resolves a review skill, compute the phase brief with the real command, and show whether the name is in it. If it IS there through a path the grep missed, stop: report where, add the pinning case only, and say so.

If it is not: file the bug in this plan (`audit-task.py bug-add`, medium) and fix it here - the phase brief gains a section naming the resolved skill and its basis exactly as `_areas.resolve_review_skill` returns them (the phase's own, an area's, or the plan's), and saying nothing when none resolves or when an explicit null stopped the fallback. One resolver, no second precedence chain. The headless reviewer session (drive-phase.py writer_argv / session_skills) must load the same skill; check whether it does and include it if not.

Allow case to pin as explicitly as the fix: a phase with no review skill, and a phase whose area sets reviewSkill null, get a brief with NO review-skill section.

Dependants: reference/phase-signoff.md and reference/orchestrator.md where they describe what the phase reviewer is handed; tools/measure-context.py ceilings for the sign-off entry; PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md's section on audit-lookup.py.

Acceptance:
1. A phase brief computed for a phase that resolves a review skill names that skill and the level it resolved from.
2. A phase with none, and one stopped by an explicit null, get no such section.
3. The headless reviewer session is started with the review skill when one resolves.
4. The bug is filed and closed by this task's commit, or the outcome says why none was owed.

NOT FIXED, OUTSIDE SCOPE, FOR THE REGISTER: reference/orchestrator.md:163-164 and PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md's audit-lookup section ('resolved skills (area first)') still describe executor skills as area first, while co1 in tests/test_audit_lookup.py pins _areas.resolve_skills as plan default, then area, then task. tasks.title: Four places where a document says what the code does not
tasks.description:
Each row was read on de21866c; RE-VERIFY each against the code before editing, and where the code turns out to agree with the document, leave the document and say so.

(a) plugins/audit/README.md, the guard-bash-writes.py row of the enforcement table (line 371 on de21866c) calls it 'non-blocking additionalContext'. plugins/audit/hooks/guard-bash-writes.py emits `"decision": "block"` (line 2253) for one class of authored path under the deny tier. Say what it does and when; SECURITY.md already describes it - the two must agree.
(b) SECURITY.md ~1260: 'Every hook has an explicit 10-second timeout.' plugins/audit/hooks/hooks.json carries one timeout of 86400 (drive-without-model). Do not write the count of hooks into prose; say which hook is the exception and why, or point at the file.
(c) SECURITY.md ~1439-1443 describes an armed #no-plan bypass as expiring with the 7-day state GC. plugins/audit/hooks/_config.py BYPASS_TTL_SECONDS is 30 * 60 and the README already says so. Make SECURITY.md say what the code does; name the constant rather than restating the figure where the lint would read it as a bare number.
(d) plugins/audit/reference/execute-task.md ~73-77 and reference/orchestrator.md ~164 give the executor's skill order as area skills then task.skills. `_areas.resolve_skills` and the schema put meta.defaultSkills first. Fix both passages to the resolver's order.

This is a documentation task under the repo's prose-number lints (`_deps.doc_prose_numbers`): read CONTRIBUTING.md 'Writing a count that is allowed' before writing any number. Dependants: tools/measure-context.py DOC_CEILINGS for reference/orchestrator.md; any tests/ case pinning these sentences (grep a distinctive phrase of each before changing it).

Acceptance:
1. README's guard-bash-writes row and SECURITY.md describe the same behaviour, and it is the code's.
2. SECURITY.md no longer claims one timeout for every hook.
3. SECURITY.md's bypass-expiry sentence matches BYPASS_TTL_SECONDS.
4. Both reference passages give the skill order `_areas.resolve_skills` implements.
5. A locking case pins (d) against the resolver's order, so the prose cannot drift from it again.

tasks.title: A pure function reads a task's diff for moves that lower the bar
tasks.description:
New module plugins/audit/scripts/governance/_floor_guard.py: given a task's unified diff against its base (and a way to read a file at the base and in the tree), return the moves that make a test easier or a checker quieter. It decides nothing and refuses nothing; a later task reports its findings.

Why: docs/research/benchmark-feature-results.md section 4.1 - the plain arm edited a protected test's existing assertion in every session; nothing in the plugin would have seen it. The red-first helper proves a NEW test can fail; the `tests-moved` refusal covers a test file changed after its proof; neither reads an existing test being weakened.

Moves to find, each a named finding with path and line:
1. a test file deleted;
2. an existing test definition changed - for Python, compare each function and method defined in the base copy of a test file with the same qualified name in the tree by `ast.dump` (line numbers excluded, so a test appended beside it is not a change), and report definitions that changed or disappeared; for other languages report assertion lines removed from a test file (expect(, assert, should, t.Error/t.Fatal - a table, not scattered regexes);
3. a skip added to a test file (pytest.mark.skip/skipif/xfail, unittest.skip*, .skip( / xit( / xdescribe( / it.todo(, t.Skip();
4. a suppression added anywhere (# noqa, # type: ignore, eslint-disable*, @ts-ignore, @ts-expect-error, istanbul ignore, nosemgrep, gitleaks:allow, Stryker disable, # pragma: no cover);
5. a stub added in non-test code (raise NotImplementedError, throw new Error('Not implemented'), an empty except/catch body).

THREE ANSWERS, AND ONLY ONE IS CLEAN: findings, clean, or could-not-tell with its reason (a diff that does not parse, a base file that cannot be read, a Python file that does not compile on either side). could-not-tell is never returned as clean and never as a finding - the same three-valued shape as _runner_collects.py, which is the model to follow.

What a test file is must come from one existing definition, not a new one: find how the plugin already classifies test paths (the plan gate's exempt test patterns in hooks/_config.py DEFAULTS, and _runner_collects / _affected_tests) and reuse the scripts-side one; say which you reused.

ALLOW CASES - pin each as explicitly as a finding, because a guard that fires on honest work is routed around: a test appended to an existing file; a test RENAMED with its body unchanged; an assertion changed in a test the task itself declares in tests.add (the caller passes the declared paths/cases - those are the task's to change and are reported as declared, not as findings); a `# noqa` that was already on the line and only moved; a comment or docstring edit inside a test; a suppression added inside a test FIXTURE string (text the test feeds to something else).

The five obligations of a new .py under scripts/ are yours (CLAUDE.md 'Adding a .py'): tests/test__floor_guard.py printing the N/M cases passed contract; a layer in tools/lints/_deps.py LAYERS; a tree line AND a section in PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md; the PATH_PREAMBLE byte for byte. It is a helper, not an entry point. Stdlib only, Python 3.8, no annotations, %-formatting.

Acceptance:
1. Each of the five moves is found on a minimal diff and carries path, line and move name.
2. Each allow case above returns no finding.
3. An unparseable diff, an unreadable base file and a non-compiling Python file each return could-not-tell with a reason, never clean.
4. A changed definition in a test the caller declared is returned as declared, apart from findings.
5. The module imports nothing outside the stdlib and its layer, and the import-graph and enumeration lints pass.

tasks.title: A refactor can prove its tests were green before the change
tasks.description:
The red-first helper (`stamp-verification.py red`, run by `drive-phase.py submit`) proves a tdd task's new test fails on the base. A behaviour-preserving refactor needs the mirror: the characterization tests it adds must PASS on the base, or they characterize the new behaviour rather than the old.

- Schema: `tests.expectGreenFirst` (boolean, optional) beside expectRedFirst in schema/audit-plan.schema.json. Absent means today's behaviour exactly. The validator (_manifest_rules.py) refuses a task that sets both expectGreenFirst true and expectRedFirst true, and one that sets it with tests.add empty - say which rule fired.
- Helper: `stamp-verification.py green`, built on the SAME throwaway tree the red verb builds (HEAD checked out, the task's declared test files copied over it) - reuse that builder, do not write a second one. proved = the command exits 0 on the base AND at least one of the task's own cases was collected and passed. A red there is `not-green` (the test does not describe the base). Zero collected, an import/compile error, or a host refusal is could-not-prove with the reason verbatim - the same vocabulary rule the red side keeps, and the same runner list.
- Filing: submit runs it when the task owes it (expectGreenFirst true) and a test command is given after `--`, and refuses an executor return on an owed task without one, as it does for red-first. The filed return gains a greenFirst block (status proved | not-green | could-not-prove | not-attempted, basis, at) written by the verb.
- Reviewer: the brief shows it; agents/audit-reviewer.md says in one line that not-green on a refactor means the tests were written to the new code (inside the ceiling - check the byte count first). A not-green answer is one only a human settles, like not-proved: follow what _filed_returns.needs_human does for red-first rather than inventing a second mechanism.
- /audit:task add: the flag that sets it, wherever expectRedFirst is set today.
- Docs: README test-discipline section, reference/execute-task.md, COMPATIBILITY.md (new field read), CHANGELOG.md, PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md.

Dependants: everything that enumerates the tests keys or the return keys (the vocabulary lints in tools/lints/_refs.py - red_first_vocabulary_drift is the model, and it or a sibling must hold the new words), the panel if it edits tests fields, audit-lookup's brief builders, examples/ manifests validated in CI.

Acceptance:
1. A task with expectGreenFirst whose added test passes on the base files greenFirst proved.
2. One whose added test fails on the base files not-green, and sign-off treats it as an answer a human settles.
3. Zero collected / compile error / refusal files could-not-prove with the reason verbatim.
4. An owed task filed without a test command is refused with the reason.
5. A plan without the field validates and behaves exactly as before; both flags true is refused by the validator.
6. The new words are held by a vocabulary lint.

tasks.title: An agent's edit-tool write to the audit config is refused or asked
tasks.description:
`.claude/**` is in the plan gate's default exemptGlobs (hooks/_config.py DEFAULTS), and no guard names `.claude/audit.config.json`. So an executor or reviewer can write `policy.enabled: false`, `planGate: "observe"` or `journal.enabled: false` with Edit/Write and the only trace is a journal row. A capability policy the governed agent can switch off is advisory. guard-edits.py already protects its neighbours the same way: rule 3 (the installed plugin's own files), rule 4 (plan-bypass state files), rule 5 (the journal).

File the bug in this plan first (`audit-task.py bug-add`, medium: present since the policy shipped, not a regression), then add rule 6 to plugins/audit/hooks/guard-edits.py:
- an edit-tool write (Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, and the MCP write payloads the hook already reads) whose target is the project's audit config - resolved through the SAME function the hooks use to find that file, never a hard-coded path - from a SUBAGENT (`_config.is_subagent`) is denied, with a reason that says the owner changes it through /audit:panel or by hand;
- the same write from the main session is `ask`: the human decides per call. Not deny - the owner legitimately asks the main session to change config.

BEFORE CHOOSING `ask`, enumerate who writes this file with an edit tool today and say so in your outcome: grep plugins/audit/commands/*.md, reference/*.md and skills/ for instructions to Edit/Write the config (init's write step is the likely one), and the panel server (it writes through its own process, not a tool - confirm). A flow the plugin itself instructs must keep working: if a command tells the model to Write the config, either that flow moves to a script verb in this task, or the prompt it now meets is named in that command's text. Do not leave a shipped command that silently meets a prompt it never mentions.

STATED LIMIT, to write down rather than hide: a shell-form write (sed -i, a redirect, an interpreter) is not covered by this rule and stays journal-only; the shell reader lives in guard-secrets-read.py and is out of scope here. SECURITY.md must say exactly that in its residuals, and its fail-mode table row for guard-edits is unchanged (internal error -> allow).

Allow cases to pin: an edit to another file under .claude/ (settings.json, a skill) is untouched by rule 6; a READ of the config is never asked; a write to a file merely NAMED audit.config.json elsewhere in the tree is untouched; in the plugin's own source checkout (the dev-mode exception rule 3 already defines) decide whether the rule applies and pin your answer - this repository edits its own .claude/audit.config.json rarely, and tests build theirs in scratch directories.

If the API refuses to produce guard code for this task, record the refusal verbatim as could-not-prove and stop; do not route around it.

Acceptance:
1. A subagent's Edit/Write to the resolved audit config is denied with a reason naming the owner's routes.
2. The main session's is `ask`.
3. The allow cases above are quiet.
4. Every command or reference text that instructs an edit-tool write of the config either no longer does or names the prompt.
5. SECURITY.md states the rule and the shell-form residual; the bug is closed by this commit.

tasks.title: The pinned skills rule and the help text name the plan default before the area
tasks.description:
SG1.3 corrected the executor's skill order in the reference files, the guide and the README to what _areas.resolve_skills builds: meta.defaultSkills, then each tag's meta.areas[tag].skills, then task.skills. Two statements of the same rule were outside its files and are still stale on the commit that closes it. (1) plugins/audit/scripts/manifest/_areas.py SKILLS_RULE is the string 'then task.skills, deduped, area first' and is pinned into reference/execute-task.md's 'Execute the task' section by the claim-drift row beside it; SG1.3 had to keep that phrase in the corrected sentence ('..., deduped, area first under the plan default') only because the constant could not change. (2) plugins/audit/scripts/config/_help.py renders 'The executor's skills are the area's, <SKILLS_RULE>' into the help endpoint's areas topic, which leaves out the plan level altogether. Make the constant state the whole order the resolver applies, in one phrase a reader can check against resolve_skills, and make the help sentence and the reference sentence carry it without the patch SG1.3 needed. Derive, do not restate: if the phrase can be composed from what the resolver itself defines, do that. Dependants you answer for: the claim-drift table in _areas.py and every reader of it (tests/test__areas.py, tools/gate-parity.py), tests/test__help.py (its areas-topic case reads SKILLS_RULE), the help topics served to the panel drawer, reference/execute-task.md (the pinned sentence; tools/measure-context.py ceilings), and tests/test__refs.py sko1-sko6, which pin the order in the documents and must stay green. docs/research/pipeline-cost-design.md also says 'resolved area first': it is a dated design record - leave it and say so.

Acceptance:
1. SKILLS_RULE names the plan default, then the area, then the task, and a case holds it to the order _areas.resolve_skills returns for a plan that sets all three.
2. The help endpoint's areas topic states that order.
3. reference/execute-task.md carries the new pinned phrase and no leftover of the old one.
4. The claim-drift lint, tests/test__help.py and sko1-sko6 are green.

add: tests/test__areas.py: SKILLS_RULE names the three levels in the order resolve_skills returns for a plan that sets all three; red on the commit that closes SG1.3
